To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) empathy has three neural components, (2) the three components are associated with different brain regions, and (3) these brain regions are predictive of real-world prosocial behavior.

(1) empathy for positive and empathy for negative emotions activate brain regions that are associated with the experience of positive and negative emotions, respectively, (2) the mirror system and the mentalizing system are differentially engaged during context-independent and context-dependent empathic responses, and (3) the septal area is a common neural substrate of empathy for pain, empathy for anxiety, and empathy for happiness, and that septal activation is predictive of real-world helping behavior.

empathy for positive or negative emotions selectively activates brain regions associated with the processing of positive or negative affect, respectively, whereas the mirror and mentalizing systems are more active during empathy to context-independent and context-dependent events, respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural components of empathy and their relationship to daily prosocial behavior.
the neural mechanisms underlying empathy and how these processes relate to daily social behaviors.
the neurocognitive mechanisms of empathy and its relation with prosocial behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neural components of empathy are: 1) affective congruency, 2) perspective taking, 3) prosocial motivation, 4) social context and 5) the amount of social context.
the septal area is the only region that is common across the three components of emotion empathy and that this region is the neural basis of prosocial motivation.
there is no conclusive statement about the neural correlates of empathy, and that future research should focus on the three components of empathic responding.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
empathy is an affective state with multiple neural components that are predictive of real-world prosocial behavior.
the neural components of empathy predict daily prosocial behavior.
we have demonstrated that there are neural systems that underlie the three components of the empathy construct, and these neural systems predict real-life prosocial behavior.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there is no single brain region that is responsible for empathy; instead, the neural systems involved in empathy depend on whether one is empathizing with a positive or negative event, as well as the social context in which that emotion occurs.
the septal area may be a neural component that underlies prosocial motivation across multiple empathic contexts.
empathy is a complex phenomenon with multiple neural substrates and motivational consequences.
